title: The Universe · Episode 3
chapters: The life and death of stars
Reading starlight: what stars are made of

units.t: The Universe. Episode three.
In this episode: The Moon: our strange companion, Eclipses: the cosmic coincidence, The life and death of stars and Reading starlight: what stars are made of.
Part one. The Moon: our strange companion.
It was born in a collision, it's slowly drifting away, and it controls the tides at your local beach.
Born in a collision.
The leading explanation is the giant-impact hypothesis.
About 4.
5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body, sometimes called Theia, smashed into the young Earth.
The collision flung molten rock into orbit, which clumped together to form the Moon.
Evidence includes the Moon's small iron core and the remarkable similarity between Apollo Moon rocks and rocks on Earth.
The dark patches you can see are called maria, Latin for 'seas', because early astronomers thought they were oceans.
They are plains of solidified lava that flooded huge impact basins roughly 3 to 3.
9 billion years ago.
With no wind, rain or moving plates, craters last billions of years.
Binoculars show bright rays spreading from young craters like Tycho.
One face, many phases.
The Moon spins once in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, about 27 days, so the same side always faces us.
Earth's gravity gradually slowed its spin until it locked into step, a process called tidal locking.
The far side isn't permanently dark; it gets just as much sunlight.
Humans first saw it in 1959, in photos from a Soviet probe.
The Moon makes no light of its own; half of it is always lit by the Sun.
As it orbits, we see different amounts of that lit half, giving the phases in a cycle of about 29.
5 days.
From Australia, the Moon appears 'upside down' compared with northern hemisphere pictures, so a waxing crescent is lit on the left.
Tides and drifting.
The Moon's gravity pulls hardest on the ocean facing it, creating a bulge, and least on the far side, where another bulge forms.
As Earth rotates through the two bulges, most coasts get two high tides a day.
When Sun and Moon line up at full and new moon, we get extra-large spring tides.
Australia's north-west has some of the world's largest tides, over 10 metres.
Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon.
Lasers fired at them show it is drifting away by about 3.
8 centimetres a year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow.
Tidal forces are also lengthening Earth's day: hundreds of millions of years ago, a day was around 22 hours.
Sun, Moon, shadow.
By a remarkable coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away, so they look almost the same size in our sky.
When the Moon passes directly in front of the Sun, it can block it completely in a total solar eclipse.
When Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, its shadow falls on the Moon, often turning it red, in a lunar eclipse.
Eclipses don't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted slightly.
As the Moon drifts away, it will look too small to cover the Sun, and total solar eclipses will end.
Who owns the Moon.
Officially, nobody owns the Moon.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, joined by Australia and more than 100 other countries, says no nation can claim the Moon or any other celestial body, and that space should be used for peaceful purposes.
But plans to mine lunar water ice raise a new question: can a company own what it digs up?

In 2020, Australia was one of eight founding signatories of the Artemis Accords, US-led principles that support using space resources and call for protecting historic sites such as the Apollo landing areas.
Dozens more countries have since signed, while China and Russia are planning their own lunar research station instead.
The key idea: The Moon most likely formed when a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth, and its dark seas are ancient lava plains.
Part two. Eclipses: the cosmic coincidence.
For a few minutes, day turns to night, the temperature drops and stars appear at noon.
It happens because of one of the luckiest coincidences in the solar system.
A perfect fit.
Hold your thumb at arm's length and it can hide a whole building.
The Moon does the same trick with the Sun.
The Sun is roughly 400 times the Moon's diameter, yet it also sits roughly 400 times farther from us.
Both discs therefore look almost exactly the same size in our sky, about half a degree across.
No other planet has a moon that fits its sun so neatly.
When the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun, it can cover the blinding disc completely and leave the faint outer atmosphere, the corona, glowing like a silver crown.
It is an accident of geometry, and we happen to live in the right era to enjoy it.
Total, annular, partial.
The Moon's orbit is not a perfect circle.
If an eclipse happens when the Moon is near its closest point, it looks big enough to cover the Sun entirely, giving a total eclipse.
Near its farthest point, the Moon looks slightly too small and a bright ring of sunlight surrounds it.
That is an annular eclipse, from the Latin annulus, meaning ring.
Anyone outside the narrow central path sees only a partial eclipse, with a bite taken out of the Sun.
The path of totality is usually only about 100 to 200 kilometres wide and races across Earth's surface faster than a jet airliner.
That is why eclipse chasers travel the world to stand in exactly the right strip of land.
Why not every month.
The Moon circles Earth roughly once a month, so you might expect an eclipse at every new moon.
The catch is that its orbit is tilted about five degrees compared with Earth's path around the Sun.
Most months the new moon slides just above or below the Sun in our sky and nothing happens.
Eclipses can only occur when a new or full moon lines up with one of the two points where the orbits cross.
These alignments arrive in eclipse seasons, roughly every six months.
Ancient Babylonian astronomers noticed that eclipses repeat in a cycle of about 18 years and 11 days, now called the saros.
It let them predict eclipses long before anyone understood orbits.
The blood moon.
In a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and the full Moon, and our planet's shadow falls across the lunar surface.
You might expect the Moon to vanish, but it usually glows deep copper or blood red.
The reason is our atmosphere.
Sunlight skimming past the edge of Earth is bent inwards towards the Moon, and most of its blue light is scattered out on the way, the same process that makes sunsets red.
In effect, the Moon is lit by every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once.
Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses can be seen by anyone on the night side of the planet, and they are completely safe to watch with the naked eye.
Watching safely.
Even when most of the Sun is covered, the remaining sliver is intense enough to damage the retina.
The retina has no pain receptors, so you may not notice until afterwards.
Ordinary sunglasses are nowhere near dark enough.

Safe options include certified eclipse glasses or solar viewers meeting the ISO 12312-2 standard, or an indirect method such as a pinhole projector, where you look at an image of the Sun cast onto paper.
Never look through binoculars, a camera or a telescope without a proper solar filter fitted to the front.
The one exception is the brief period of totality, when the Sun is completely hidden.
The moment the first bead of sunlight reappears, the glasses go back on.
Australia's turn comes on 22 July 2028, when totality crosses the country, including Sydney.
The key idea: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so they look almost the same size.
Part three. The life and death of stars.
How stars are born, why their mass decides their fate, and why many of them don't shine alone.
Born in clouds.
Stars form inside giant, cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, made mostly of hydrogen.
Something, perhaps a nearby supernova or a collision between clouds, disturbs the gas.
Gravity pulls denser clumps together, and as they shrink they heat up.
When the core reaches about 10 million degrees, nuclear fusion ignites and a star is born.
The Orion Nebula, a fuzzy patch in Orion's 'sword', the handle of the Saucepan in Australian skies, is a stellar nursery you can see with the naked eye.
The Sun and starlight.
In a star's core, hydrogen nuclei are squeezed so hard they fuse into helium, converting a little mass into a lot of energy.
The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of matter into energy every second.
That outward push balances gravity pulling inwards, and for most of a star's life the two stay locked in balance.
The Sun is a fairly ordinary star, 4.
6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its life.
Its surface is about 5,500 degrees, its core about 15 million °C. Energy can take tens of thousands of years to leave the core, then about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Colour shows temperature: reddish Antares is cooler, blue-white Rigel hotter.
Mass decides fate.
A star's mass decides its colour, brightness and lifespan.
Small, cool red dwarfs use fuel so slowly they can shine for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed.
Most stars in the galaxy are red dwarfs, too faint to see by eye.
Massive blue stars burn hot and fast and last only a few million years: more fuel means a shorter life.
In about 5 billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant, perhaps engulfing Mercury, Venus and possibly Earth.
Long before then, in about a billion years, its growing brightness will have boiled away Earth's oceans.
It will puff off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf: a dense, Earth-sized ember that cools over trillions of years.
The death of a giant.
Massive stars end far more violently.
They fuse heavier and heavier elements in their cores, up to iron.
Fusing iron doesn't release energy, so the core collapses in less than a second and rebounds in a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine a galaxy of billions of stars.
The collapsed core becomes a neutron star, so dense that a teaspoon would weigh billions of tonnes, or, if massive enough, a black hole.
Stars in pairs.
Our solitary Sun is a little unusual: close to half of Sun-like stars have at least one companion.
Algol, in Perseus, dims noticeably every 2.
9 days as a fainter partner crosses in front of it.
Sirius is circled by a small, faint white dwarf, Sirius B.
When a white dwarf pulls enough gas from a close partner, or merges with another white dwarf, it can blow apart in a type Ia supernova.
These reach a predictable peak brightness, so astronomers use them to measure distances across the universe, work that earned ANU's Brian Schmidt a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The key idea: Stars form in nebulae when gravity pulls gas together until the core ignites nuclear fusion.
Part four. Reading starlight: what stars are made of.
In 1835 a famous philosopher declared that we could never know what the stars are made of.
Within a few decades, scientists were doing exactly that, using rainbows.
An impossible question.
The French philosopher Auguste Comte, founder of positivism, wanted science to stick to what could be observed.

In 1835 he gave an example of knowledge forever beyond reach: we could study the stars' shapes, distances and motions, but never their chemical composition, since no one could visit them or take a sample.
It seemed reasonable.
Chemistry meant handling substances in a laboratory, and the stars were unreachably far away.
Yet within about 25 years, scientists found a way to identify elements in the Sun from Earth.
Comte's claim is now often quoted as a warning that 'impossible' can be a dangerous word.
The key had already been found, in a ray of sunlight split by glass.
Dark lines in the rainbow.
Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow, a spectrum.
In 1814, German optician Joseph von Fraunhofer built instruments precise enough to magnify it and found hundreds of thin dark lines, as if exact colours were missing.
He mapped about 570 and labelled the strongest with letters, a system still used.
He could not explain them.
Around 1859 in Heidelberg, physicist Gustav Kirchhoff and chemist Robert Bunsen heated substances in a flame and studied the light through a prism.
Each element gave its own set of bright lines, like a barcode.
Sodium's two yellow lines matched two of Fraunhofer's dark lines.
Cooler gas in the Sun's outer layers absorbs those same colours, so dark lines reveal which elements are present.
Helium, found in sunlight.
During a total solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers studying the Sun's glowing outer layers saw a bright yellow line that matched no known element.
Jules Janssen observed it from India, and Norman Lockyer studied it soon afterwards.
Lockyer, working with chemist Edward Frankland, concluded it belonged to a new element and named it helium, after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun.
Many chemists were sceptical of an element known only from a distant star.
Then in 1895 Scottish chemist William Ramsay detected the same spectral line from gas released by a uranium mineral.
Helium, the second most common element in the universe, had first been discovered 150 million kilometres away.
The method also found two new elements on Earth, caesium and rubidium.
Cecilia Payne's discovery.
In the early 1900s astronomers assumed stars had about the same make-up as Earth's crust, rich in heavier elements like iron.
Cecilia Payne, a young British astronomer who moved to Harvard because women had few prospects in astronomy in England, applied new atomic physics to stellar spectra.
Her 1925 doctoral thesis concluded that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, in vastly greater amounts than anyone expected.
The senior astronomer Henry Norris Russell persuaded her to describe the result as almost certainly not real.
A few years later Russell reached the same conclusion himself.
Payne was right: hydrogen and helium make up about 98 per cent of the ordinary matter in stars.
Her thesis is now considered among the most important in astronomy.
Colour, temperature, motion.
Spectra hold far more than a list of ingredients.
A star's colour reveals its surface temperature: red stars are relatively cool, around 3,000 degrees, while blue-white stars can exceed 20,000 degrees.
In the early 1900s, Annie Jump Cannon at Harvard classified hundreds of thousands of stars by spectrum into the sequence O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest, which astronomers still use.
Spectra also reveal motion through the Doppler effect.
Light from an object moving away is stretched towards the red end, while light from one approaching is squeezed towards blue.
Measuring these tiny shifts showed that distant galaxies are rushing away from us, the evidence for an expanding universe, and it still helps detect planets around other stars.
The key idea: In 1835 Auguste Comte called the chemistry of the stars forever unknowable, a reminder that 'impossible' is a dangerous word.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What evidence supports the idea that a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth?
Answer. Moon rocks closely resemble rocks on Earth.
Question two. Why do the Sun and Moon look almost the same size from Earth?
Answer. The Sun is 400 times larger but 400 times farther away.
Question three. What balances the pull of gravity inside a star like the Sun?
Answer. The push of energy released by hydrogen fusion.
Question four. What lesson is Auguste Comte's 1835 claim often used to illustrate?
Answer. Calling something unknowable can be wrong.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
